articleTitle: Advantages and disadvantages of outsourcing
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The advantages and disadvantages of outsourcing technical communications services depend greatly on point of view. This paper examines outsourcing from the perspectives of the corporate buyer of services, the supplier of services, and the individual technical communicator. Successful outsourcing is assured only if the differing interests of all participants are balanced correctly.

articleTitle: Workplace communications skills and the value of communications and information use skills instruction-engineering students' perspectives
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Studies indicate that communications and information-related activities take up a substantial portion of an engineer's work week; therefore, effective communications and information use skills are one of the key engineering competencies that recent graduates of engineering programs are expected to possess. Feedback from industry rates communications and information use skills high in terms of their importance to engineering practice; however, this same feedback rates the communications and information use skills of entry-level engineers low. Missing from current discussions of communications and information use skills and competencies for engineering students is a clear explanation from the professional engineering community about what constitutes "acceptable and desirable communications and information norms" within that community. To gather adequate and generalizable data about communications and information skills instruction and to provide a student perspective on the communications skills of engineers, we undertook a national study of aerospace engineering students in March 1993. The study included questions about the importance of certain communications and information skills to professional success, the instruction students had received in these skills, and perceived helpfulness of the instruction. Selected results from the student study are reported.

articleTitle: Developing online writing aids for electrical engineering majors-a progress report
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: In 1993, we presented our framework for a five-year project to enhance the communication skills of electrical engineering students and in 1994 we discussed our findings of our initial surveys of electrical engineering students and a study of communication activities of recent graduates in a high tech company. In this paper we discuss the functions of our instructional programs, demonstrate the initial program interfaces that we have developed, discuss our development process, report the results of initial usability testing of the programs, and discuss selected survey results of electrical engineers' communication practices.

articleTitle: From user's mental models to information system's specification and vice versa by extended visual notation
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The paper discusses how a story-telling theory and a related visual tool can support communication between users and analyst in developing an effective information systems design. To this end the paper firstly surveys approaches to requirements engineering from the communication point of view, then introduces a multimedia-based template as a tool to facilitate the construction of a shared mental model of the system between user and designer, and finally illustrates a case study and outlines some possible extensions of the proposed approach.

articleTitle: Testing the comprehensibility of Simplified English: an analysis of airplane procedure documents
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The experiment reported was conducted to determine whether procedures written in Simplified English (SE) would be more effective than their non-SE counterparts. This study examined the effect of document type (SE versus non-SE), passage (Document A versus Document B), and native language (native versus non-native English speakers) on the comprehensibility, identification of content location, and task completion time of procedure documents for airplane maintenance. This research indicates that SE significantly improves the comprehensibility and the identification of content location of more complex documents for both native and non-native speakers.

articleTitle: Technology and changes in higher education
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Economic and technological changes are occurring at an accelerating rate in our information-based society, making lifelong learning for most adults a necessity. There is, however, a relative imbalance between the demanded pace of change for students and faculty compared to that in the curriculum and institutions of higher education. The paper suggests that technology needs to become as interwoven in institutional strategic planning and educational delivery as it is in society-to become an integral part of teaching and learning throughout the student's life-long learning environment.

articleTitle: Applying multimedia to technical information
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The value of multimedia is that users can receive information in the medium most appropriate to the content and its intended use. In addition to our usual store of words and graphics, we as communicators can use images, sound, animation, and video if those media are appropriate to the message and audience. For example, if motion aids what we are trying to explain, video or animation would be appropriate media to use; audio can help provide emphasis; graphics and animation can greatly help explain concepts; images can provide realism; 3-D animation can be extremely useful at illustrating hardware or procedures for hardware that does not yet exist. As a community, however, we're still working out details about the role that multimedia can and should play in technical information: When is it appropriate to use multimedia? Which media are appropriate to a given situation? Although much research has been done on media and learning, there currently exists no definitive media selection model as it applies to technical communication. It's a complex topic, but we offer some suggestions.

articleTitle: Who are we? Why do we act the way we do? An overview of the Myers Briggs personality type indicator
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Throughout the ages, people have attempted to understand, explain and/or categorize the similarities and differences of human behavior. The Ancient Greeks labeled individuals using the four designations of sanguine, choleric, phlegmatic and melancholic. The American Plains Indians categorized people according to the four points of the compass. Astrology's birth signs have for centuries been a popular system of labeling similar characteristics in human behavior. This paper is an introduction to the theory of classifying personality types first presented by the Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung. In the 1920's, two Americans, Katherine Cook-Briggs and Isabel Briggs-Myers began their life-long study of individual differences which led to the development of the Myers-Briggs type indicator. This inventory of preferences has evolved to be a well-respected psychological tool that is perhaps the most widely used world-wide.

articleTitle: Graphics: the missing half of technical communication
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Technical communicators must make graphics a full partner of words in the process of communication. Why? Because in this age of television it is graphics alone that often determines whether the prose itself will get read. The first step is to debunk some of the myths that inhibit the use of graphics in technical communication. The second step is to conduct hands-on workshops.

articleTitle: Gathering and implementing market-driven requirements
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Future success for any business or operation means understanding what the market wants and needs. Not only this, in our world, one must bring the product or service to the market faster than the the competition. The paper presents a method for discovering, systematically gathering, and implementing marketplace wants and needs. How to determine what must be offered to meet and to beat the competition to the future is also practiced.

articleTitle: The rhetoric of e-mail: an analysis of style
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The paper presents the results of a stylistic analysis of 200 samples of e-mail memoranda gathered from four organizations. Through systematic counting of textual features such as sentence and paragraph length, grammatical types of sentence, and word choice, the study examines patterns of rhetorical choice common to electronic mail. In this sample, short serial sentences dominated, and writers preferred active verbs over other forms, indicating composing processes for e-mail are rudimentary and somewhat spontaneous.

articleTitle: Team building in an organizational setting
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Examines the concept of team building in organizational settings. Team building is a form of social organization which seems to be replacing the traditional system of management. Two major components are introduced-the utilization of a facilitator and an emphasis on enhancing communication skills. Introducing a facilitator to coordinate activities between management and a team serves to clarify the team's purpose and keep an open line of communication. A second emphasis is on the education of team members on the principles of small group communication. Six small group communication variables are introduced and the role of the facilitator in each is highlighted.

articleTitle: The paperless office: facts and fictions
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: With the advent of computers, many have anticipated the realization of the "paperless" office. Despite the technology that makes an electronic office feasible, the proliferation of paper continues. The paper suggests a "less" paper office serves as a more realistic goal than the "paperless" office. Case examples show two organizations attempts to use technology to reduce paper: one successfully, one unsuccessfully. The author suggests a three phase implementation strategy to help organizations use technology to reduce paper and costs and increase productivity.

articleTitle: Instructional system design: its role in coast guard training and how it can influence the development of training materials
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Instructional system design (ISD) is a systematic approach to the design and development of performance based training. The key principles of ISD are: identifying what human performance needs to be changed, identifying the outcomes of the instruction, developing the instruction, implementing the instruction and evaluating the instruction's effectiveness. Using the principles of ISD, the US Coast Guard has developed a five step model to develop performance based training programs. This ISD model also provides a different approach to the development of training materials, lending itself to a type of backward or reverse planning which can easily be adapted to develop various types of non-military training materials.

articleTitle: Motivating the writing process: who says engineers have no emotions?
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The process of writing technical papers is examined from the prospective of both the engineer and industry. The motivation for working in any esoteric specialty centers around purpose fulfillment and colleague acceptance. This poses a management challenge, namely how to recognize the engineering writing environment and achieve the organization's technical objectives in a way that also fulfills the writer's needs. The engineer must believe that the effort of writing will be rewarded. Mentors, who encourage younger engineers, also need to be properly nurtured. Both the engineer and the employer benefit by gaining experience and exposure.

articleTitle: Color me blue...or red or green? Lessons from the literature on color and usability
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Color is a complex and powerful phenomenon that can have profound effects on human beings. With the spread of low-cost color technology, many technical communicators, interface designers, and others have the ability to use color in their work, but they may lack basic knowledge of how to use color effectively for their audiences. This paper surveys the literature in technical communication and psychology and suggests ways that color can be used to improve the usability of documents and interfaces.

articleTitle: Multimedia law: speedbump or brick wall for multimedia projects?
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Developers need to contend with more than content and tools when they make multimedia products. They have to ensure that their product does not infringe on someone's copyrights, trademarks, moral rights or rights of privacy and publicity. The paper describes the laws that apply to multimedia and suggests how to avoid legal obstacles on multimedia projects.

articleTitle: Theory versus application: finding the right combination in academic programs
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Finding the best combination of theoretical versus applied topics in communication programs is difficult. Knowing how that mix may differ for undergraduate and graduate students is also a challenge. Communicators in primarily high-tech industries were surveyed to elicit their input on which courses or areas of knowledge were the most important or useful to their job performance. Additional survey data came from a group of Florida Tech communication alumni. Their responses reveal that a combination of theoretical and applied work is necessary to provide adequate background knowledge and practical skills for successful performance in the workplace.

articleTitle: Nominalizations: effect on recall and comprehension
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: This study evaluated the effects of nominalizations (verbs that have been transformed into nouns) used in technical documents on subjects' recall and comprehension. Subjects read one of four technical passages (one of two texts, a nominalized or denominalized version) and took a recall and a comprehension test. Results indicate that nominalizations critical to the central meaning of the passage affected recall. Comprehension was not affected by nominalization/denominalization.

articleTitle: The populist of science
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The need for members of the public to understand science is increasing rapidly. Science underlies the technology that is changing our jobs, our homes, and our lives. It also bears on many of the political issues we must decide, especially in the area of the environment and its restoration. Scientists, however, are often uncomfortable with addressing the public. This paper describes a number of ways that scientists can share their science with the public and give the public the information it needs to make sound decisions.

articleTitle: Writing in the university engineering community: a multi-year program at University of California, Santa Barbara
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The paper describes a network of instructional activities based on several years of planning between the Writing Program and the College of Engineering at University of California, Santa Barbara. The goal was to saturate the curriculum with opportunities for student engineers at all levels-freshman to graduate-to acquire strong communication skills. We wanted writing instruction to be thoroughly contextualized and to provide students with multiple literacies: print; non-print; multimedia; oral; visual.

articleTitle: Virtual blood, real sweat, no tears: lessons learned from making a publication about electronic publications
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The EIA Electronic Document Report (EDR) provides critical information and informed perspective for business people concerned with the role that electronic information will play in meeting the business objectives of enhanced performance and competitiveness. As publishers, we use the very technology and tools that the EDR describes for developing, managing, delivering, and using electronic documents. Creating an electronic publication about electronic documents required that we address readers' requirements as well as our own as publishers, develop and implement the right information model, assemble a top-notch staff, and, in essence, develop a radically new publication methodology. The EIA Electronic Document Report (EDR) is a diskette-based publication that provides critical information and informed perspective about the development, management, delivery, and use of electronic documents as a key requirement of modern business. But the EDR is more than just a new publication about electronic documents. It is a new kind of publication that employs the very technology and tools it describes, and making it work forced us to address the very issues that form its primary editorial content. In doing so, we had to go beyond the current vision of electronic document delivery and reject some of its prevailing tenets. Our experience with the first three issues forced us to rethink some of our own assumptions, too, but our insistence on moving beyond the current paradigm helped us avoid some serious technical and production problems, opened new business opportunities, and may give us a competitive edge in the future.

articleTitle: Why don't engineers write performance specifications?
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: This paper discusses two reasons why engineers may be reluctant to specify products strictly in terms of performance. The first is a consequence of responsibility for the implied warranty that accompanies engineering specifications. Even though only a functional description of the product may be needed in the specifications, this responsibility necessitates detailed knowledge of applicable designs to ensure that the set of performance requirements specified can actually be met. The second reason is based on the length constraint for such documents, and a simple method is suggested for preventing difficulties that may result from that constraint.

articleTitle: Workshop-Business Meeting Strategy: Presenting Information for Maximum Impact
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The workshop will focus on strategies that meeting participants can use to speed up and increase the efficiency of office, society, and business meetings they attend. Although it will discuss the role of all meeting participants, it will place most emphasis on the meeting member who has to prepare and present information at a meeting.

articleTitle: Using electronic communication to implement a multi-location software development project
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The paper discusses a two person development effort where one developer resided in San Francisco and the other was located in Cincinnati. The team met once at the beginning for two days and toward the end of the project for less than a day. The design was refined to its current form through prototyping and iterative usability testing. All levels of management and users have widely accepted the resulting product. The primary communication paths were the telephone and Lotus Notes. The resulting team synergy and critical success factors are further detailed.

articleTitle: Are your communication skills good enough
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The importance, effectiveness, and success of undergraduate communication courses in preparing students for workplace communication tasks were the main issues addressed in a survey administered to business students at Florida Institute of Technology (Florida Tech). Overall, both groups felt that such tasks were important and would like to be better prepared for them in their job assignments. While over half of the graduate students believed their communication courses were adequate, the seniors felt more emphasis needs to be on work-related assignments. Adding more work-related content and specialized courses could increase student motivation by making benefits of assignments tangible. Survey results provide insights to curriculum designers who want to adequately prepare tomorrow's communicators.

articleTitle: The slim WITT diet
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: During the port of a software testing product to a new environment, we revamped our product information to meet our customers' demands by: reducing the number of books; providing more examples; and putting the information where the users need it. Before we changed our information structure, we researched industry trends, competitors, and customer preference. We then categorized our information and determined the type of information we wanted to present in online help, interactive tutorial, or book form. A particular challenge was balance: how to limit redundancy, but put the information where the customer expects to find it. We followed a plan but modified it as we went along. We conducted usability testing during our information development cycle to verify that we were on track. This paper documents our information development process. We share the whats and whys of what we did.

articleTitle: Ensuring smooth sailing: an overview of project planning and control
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The discipline of project management has evolved slowly over the last century; and it has only recently been discovered and embraced by the business community at large. Project planning and control is one aspect of project management. It is concerned with providing the answers to five basic questions: what am I producing (outputs/goals); how do I get the work done (the steps in the process); what do I need (resources); when do I need it (the schedule); and how am I doing (are things going as planned?) This paper provides an introduction to the basic techniques of project planning and control that assist the user in answering these questions. These techniques are enhanced by graphical tools that aid in organizing, presenting, and understanding the information. Once thought of primarily in the context of large construction projects, the techniques have also demonstrated their usefulness in many other situations where deadlines must be met and costs justified, monitored, and controlled.

articleTitle: The reader as explorer: tools for textual navigation
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The message in a composition should be as accessible as possible. If the reader is conceived of as an explorer through a new realm of information, the writer can devise a map that will aid the reader in his or her navigation through the composition. An accessible composition provides visual cues to permit the reader to continuously apprehend the underlying structure and reorient himself or herself. Three design features can help the writer to improve the reader's ability to access the message: a perceptible structure, the use of mnemonics, and a clear visual pathway.

articleTitle: Information access for visually impaired persons: do we still keep a "document" in "documentation"?
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: At the same time that global economies and multimedia technologies provide impetus for increasingly visual communication, the information needs of persons with limited vision may require communication to shift from graphics back to text, or on to audio or tactile forms. To understand documentation issues related to this shift, one must understand the varied forms of visual impairment, available assistive technologies, and the resultant design considerations. Efforts to prepare more effective materials for visually impaired users may yield "universal design" benefits by identifying and reducing sources of confusion for all users.

articleTitle: Are we looking for content in all the wrong places? The significance of human factors research for complex tasks in documentation
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: For complex tasks and problems, users need instructional content that differs in kind from the information in current documentation. To develop this content, writers need to adopt new contextual perspectives on tasks similar to the views in much recent research in interface design. These perspectives alter current assumptions about learning, performance, and the nature of instructional information for mental models, procedural steps, and errors.

articleTitle: Intellectual property ABCs: what communicators need to know
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Intellectual property (IP) is the most valuable asset a company has, and communication is at the heart of IP protection. Therefore, it behooves communicators to know enough about IP to ask the right questions before beginning work on an assignment. Communicators who are knowledgeable can play an important role in IP protection: they can alert the inventor to some of the pitfalls along the way; and they can become another safety net in the chain of IP protection.

articleTitle: Building quality and usability into products and processes
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Quality is an important concern, but official quality programs frequently seem directed very much towards manufacturing. The paper presents a quality model for a publications department based on criteria appropriate to technical publications.

articleTitle: The visual component of communication: influencing multiple levels of audience response
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Our audiences respond to the visual format of our information on multiple levels, making judgments about the content it contains before they read the text. This paper examines these multiple levels of visual meaning and suggests that we can use this understanding to more effectively anticipate and direct different aspects of audience response and performance.

articleTitle: Visual thinking: reassessing the communication paradigm
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The revolution that has accompanied the technological advances of the past twenty years has created a new area within the discipline of communication: visual communication. The objectives of this workshop are as follows: (1) to provide participants with a basic introduction to visual communication; (2) to acquaint participants with issues involved with visual literacy; and (3) to encourage participants in their own visual thinking through hands-on activities.

articleTitle: Leadership and the communication of change in public policy
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: With all its complexity, politics provides a fascinating array of communication relationships. The government of the Province of Alberta in Canada has embarked upon a program to eliminate deficit budgeting by a massive restructuring of the public sector. Changes of this magnitude cause uncertainty and the response of citizens is partially dependent on the communication strategies used. Innovative methods are being used to communicate the reasons why change is necessary and to consult with the public and experts to involve, obtain cooperation, and elicit feedback to advise government ministers.

articleTitle: Information communication technology R&D capability development
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: For many years it was believed that R&D researchers should be self-trained. The belief was pervasive in both academic institutions and R&D laboratories that individuals are left alone to float or sink. The Information Communication Institute of Singapore (ICIS) has developed an R&D capability development model based on experience from its MSc courses in Communication Software Management. This is a 3-stage model guiding the researchers and organizations through a comprehensive R&D project life cycle. This paper describes details of the 3 stages and its implementation.

articleTitle: The development of an in-house style guide
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: In developing the first firmwide style guide for Dames & Moore, we focused on two primary goals-presenting material that the users will be interested in and making sure that the content of the style guide itself adheres to every single prescribed "rule". We think we have guaranteed staff interest in the style guide because we answer frequently asked questions and use samples from Dames & Moore reports. We hope we have met our second goal by both internal and external quality control checks. This paper describes the content of the style guide and how our choices in determining content and maintaining quality relate to acceptance by Dames & Moore engineers, geologists and environmental scientists.

articleTitle: Technical presentation workshop: how to wow the critics
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Presentations are more than on-stage performances. They are total theatrical productions requiring you to fill four roles: script writer, producer, director, and performer. Presentations can showcase your technical expertise-gaining you respect and acclaim, or they can embarrass you-revealing your lack of communication skills. Write a good script, perfect your visuals, know your lines, act the part, and you'll shine. If you fail as writer, producer, director, or performer; your entire production will be a flop. This workshop will hone your presentation skills by focusing on these four essential roles.

articleTitle: A case study of organizational influences on writers at worldwide computer corporation
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: This paper focuses on corporate influences on writers' revision choices: Do writers internalize knowledge about corporate expectations and tacitly use that knowledge in making revision choices? The researcher, using ethnographic techniques, collected writing samples from two writers and conducted discourse-based interviews with them. Analyses of the writers' samples and interviews established that the writers' decisions partly relied on their tacit organizational knowledge.

articleTitle: Teaching technical communication with the community model: some questionable side effects
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The paper traces the development of the communication model of community as a framework for teaching technical writing. It first explores the idea of community discourse conventions as they were adapted from T.S. Kuhn's (1970) model of "normal science" within an autonomous scientific community. It then adds the idea of unconventional discourse practice within the community, as adapted from Kuhn's model of "revolutionary science." The paper argues that teaching technical writing using only discourse conventions inhibits a students' ability to contribute to innovations and change within an organizational community. Adding a critical component to the teaching better prepares students to contribute to the community's continual improvement over the long term.

articleTitle: Educating technical professionals to communicate
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Presenting salient information, significant to the audience, in an understandable manner is effective communication. Presenting information, or presenting in a manner not attuned to the audience is counter productive. Technical schools that help their students learn good information transfer and presentation techniques help them become effective communicators, which will enhance their careers. This paper addresses the following aspects of communication: know the audience you're communicating to; some basics for effective communication; communication training for technical people; and, in conclusion.

articleTitle: The translatability of Simplified English in procedure documents
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: A collaborative research project tested the translatability of a restricted language called Simplified English (SE) as it is used in maintenance procedure documents in the airline industry. The project was sponsored by the Boeing Company and conducted by University of Washington researchers, as well as members of the Boeing Information and Support Services and Boeing Commercial Airplane Group, Customer Services Division. The study examined the effect of document type (SE versus non-SE) and passage (Document A versus Document B) on the translatability of these documents. Native speakers of Chinese, Spanish, or Japanese read and translated either the SE or non-SE version of one of two procedures. Independent raters then assessed the quality of the translations. Initial results show that SE compliant documents lead to better translations in certain languages.

articleTitle: Newsletter publishing
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: When the decision to publish a newsletter is made, several questions immediately pop to mind: Should we use a one-, two-, or three-column format? How should we use white space? What color stock and ink should we use? What type families should we use? What kind of illustrations should we include? What size format should we employ? What name should we give it? What should the masthead look like? How will it be distributed? These questions, although important in their own right, are the wrong ones to start with. Rather, one should ask: Who will underwrite the costs of production? What does the sponsor want to accomplish with this newsletter? Who will be the audience(s)? What are the information needs of the readers? Where do the readers' information needs and the interests of the sponsor overlap? Only with solid answers to these latter questions will the editor/publisher of the newsletter be able to determine the need to be visually engaging, the appropriate information density, the appropriate depth of information to be presented, the optimum lengths of articles, the requisite format and design, and the subject scope of the articles to be included.

articleTitle: Workshop: Creating Action-Getting Reports and Proposals
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The workshop will focus on proven methods for writing effective, action-getting reports and proposals, particularly those technical communicators are most likely to write. Emphasis will be placed on the types of proposals independent consultants prepare for existing and potential clients.

articleTitle: Helping new users use help
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Unfamiliarity with online help systems is a major stumbling block to using application help productively. This paper suggests that help writers should address the least capable user in their product's "How to use help" topic rather than presuming that the novice user will "figure it out" or that they will learn it from the operating system. Ultimately, helping new users learn how to use the online help system makes them more productive and enhances their opinion of the product they are trying to use.

articleTitle: Cross-platform help products-the Andyne solution
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: This paper describes the development of a cross-platform online help solution used at Andyne Computing Limited for one product. The paper describes what we expected to achieve, what twists and turns the development process took, our future goals, and implications for other multi-platform products.

articleTitle: The Project Archival Navigator: a new tool for presenting and archiving information
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: The Project Archival Navigator (PAN) software is a new way of presenting and archiving information on a PC. Developed under the auspices of an Air Force laser experiment and originally used to present and archive experiment results, its authors, Applied Technology Associates (ATA), envision commercial markets for the PAN. Towards this end, this technical writer/editor was part of a team tasked with the responsibility to create a corporate capabilities presentation using the PAN, which would serve as a demo package for potential customers and investors. This paper describes technical aspects of building the PAN presentation, commercialization activities, and future plans.

articleTitle: The technical communicator as independent scholar
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Technical communicators are ideally suited for contributing serious independent research and scholarship. Their experience in providing clear technical information brings them in touch with many technical disciplines. An expertise often develops in a technical subject area through assimilation, self-education, or passion (or a combination of these elements), which frequently leads to scholarly achievement and recognition from peers and larger audiences. Outside of on-the-job contributions, partnerships with think tanks, academic- and government-affiliate research institutions offer opportunities for technical communicators to become independent scholars. The paper examines the various contributions technical communicators can make to independent scholarly research, attaining recognition for their efforts, and starting a local independent scholars' network.

articleTitle: Conducting mail and telephone surveys
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Summary form only given, substantially as follows. More and more professional communicators are using surveys to learn more about their audiences and to assess technical communication products, and yet, few communication professionals have had the opportunity to learn how to conduct surveys. Handled carefully, mail and telephone surveys can provide practicing communicators an effective, professional research technique for gathering detailed and useful information about their readers and evaluating their technical communications. This paper provides an understanding of the survey process and its major pitfalls and how to avoid them. I begin with an overview of the survey process and then elaborate on selected activities: planning, questionnaire development, sampling, data collection alternatives, coding and data analysis. Specifically, I discuss strategies for developing specific objectives, drafting and ordering questions, pre-testing the questionnaire, revising the questionnaire and producing the questionnaire; explain random vs. non-random sampling, applications and limitations, and their influence on data interpretation; explore strategies for selecting the appropriate data analysis, developing a code book, coding data and analyzing data; and detail common problems including a closer look at leading questions, double-barreled questions, overlapping categories, loaded questions, long, complex questions, jargon and negative questions.

articleTitle: Educating the technical communication professional of tomorrow
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Educating technical communicators who are prepared for tomorrow requires program planners to rethink old paradigms of curricular content, instruction delivery, tools and technologies. Programs can be designed to challenge students and to meet industry's needs, now and in the future. The authors describe the bachelor's, master's, and certificate programs at Mercer.

articleTitle: People, time and money: organizing your resources for a successful publishing project
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Regardless of whether you are producing a traditional print document, developing online help systems, or designing a home page for the Internet, you still must organize a project team, develop a schedule, and establish a budget. This workshop identifies characteristics of successful projects, involves participants in identifying real world trouble-spots that can sabotage success, and presents some industry "best practices". This workshop is appropriate for anyone responsible for producing documentation-whether you do it alone, manage an in-house staff, or coordinate outside resources.

articleTitle: Conducting and publishing integrated assessments
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Several assessments of such large-scale environmental concerns have been conducted. One was the National Acid Precipitation Assessment Program (NAPAP), which guided the drafting of the Clean Air Act. These efforts have come to be referred to as integrated assessments. In the United States, the concept of an integrated assessment has been strongly supported by the Committee on Environment and Natural Resources and by the Office of Science and Technology Policy. Despite these endorsements (and political calls to require integrated assessments of major environmental concerns), the concept of what an integrated assessment is is still hazy. The author discusses the planning of an integrated assessment and its documents.

articleTitle: Cross-disciplinary teams and the role of the technical writer
publicationTitle: 1995 IEEE International Professional Communication Conference. IPCC 95 Proceedings. Smooth Sailing to the Future
abstract: Integrating the technical writer into the product development team enhances the ease of use of the product, the timing, depth, and impact of the documentation, and results in the entire package fitting together in a more coherent fashion. The paper explores how one team worked together on a project that included the documentation in the product definition. The paper covers each point with examples from the experience of being a technical writer on the team.
